CASE STUDY ANALYSIS PART C Bharat Jain has worked for an MNC for a year now, but he has still not got used to the manner in which his team members attended his meetings. He expected them to be well prepared with the items on the agenda that he circulated at least 2 days in advance. He was very particular about this. After all he was the Project manager responsible for the completion of the project on time. He had to keep meeting his team regularly to keep a tab on the progress of the assigned work. It was difficult for Bharat to understand why his team never took his meetings seriously. The team, on the other hand, was never sure when the meetings would be called. The members grumbled that some meetings came within days of each other, whereas other meetings might be months apart. They were a little uncomfortable with Bharat’s managerial style. That day Bharat decided to hold a meeting at 12 noon, instead of 3.30 in the afternoon. It was urgent. It was 12.00 and no one was in sight. A flustered Bharat telephoned to find out what was happening. He asked one of the team members the reason for the delay. The person did not know. Bharat’s team assembled in the meeting room only by 12. 15. As usual, they arrived 15 minutes late, apologizing for the delay. As they settled, Bharat realized that they had not even read the agenda that was sent to them 2 days in advance. Their blank looks irritated him. He said, “It’s been a while since our last meeting, and I felt like we all needed to catch up on what was going on in the department and related areas in the organization.” Bharat looked away at his team as he spoke and caught one of them rolling her eyes. All of his meetings always started like this. Every time, he expressed his desire to discuss things happening, he experienced a half —hearted response from the team Anyway, Bharat went around the table and began to talk about the importance of project management. This was a favourite topic that he loved to talk on and his team must have heard him several times on this. Of course, the team noted that Bharat would include a lot of related points like interactive project planning, time management, work discipline, and realistic integrated schedule But this time he was very specific about one particular issue—how to cut down procedural details about work and concentrate on the main work so that both work efficiency improved and clear information reached customers, clients, vendors, inter-

I was planning to work late night on the XYX project you assigned me last week. I can’t do both. Besides, we have an urgent problem to take care of VIP service programme. The VIP service programme was initiated by Bharat a few months ago. The intent of the programme was honourable: to provide the best service possible. However, in practice, the programme was a nightmare. It obligated anyone in the department to stop whatever work they were doing in order to fix a problem of any magnitude. Bharat thought this was a very noble thing to do for the organization. Bharat paused for a moment and looked away at Hemlata. “Hemlata”, he said, “you know that you haven’t had much experience with this project and what you might suggest may not really work. So let’s forget about this programme. It doesn’t really matter whether we improve our image with others in the organization and also with our customers. I had thought by initiating the VIP programme, I was being customer- friendly and courteous to all. Let’s forget it.” Bharat looked away at the group. Somewhere the rhythm of communication seemed broken. Yet he continued. “Now let’s see. Since you have not had a look at the agenda, let me invite suggestions or new ideas from you all on any topic that has caught your attention.” There were no volunteers, and Bharat had to do some considerable coaxing to receive any additional comments. text: Case Study Analysis Tokyo Disneyland, the largest amusement park in Japan, draws nearly as many visitors each year as the Magic Kingdom here in the United States. But like all theme parks, the Tokyo park understood the need to offer fresh attractions and exciting new rides to keep the crowds coming back year after year. In its search for dynamic new ideas to expand its already popular park, Tokyo Disneyland turned to Walt Disney Imagineering. Generating and implementing new ideas for the Disney theme parks are tasks of Walt Disney Imagineering, the research, design, and engineering subsidiary of Walt Disney Attractions. Although Tokyo Disneyland is a Disney theme park and Disney retains the creative control of the park, the park is actually owned and operated by the Oriental Land Company. This company makes all financial and investment decisions. While creative concepts come from Disney Imagineering teams, those ideas are not automatically accepted by theme park owners. Imagineering teams not only had to dream up exciting concepts for the Tokyo park, but they also had to sell the ideas and a win the approval of Japanese owners. Millions of dollars of contracts and hundreds of jobs in the United States and in Japan rested on successful presentations to the owners of Tokyo Disneyland. Jon Georges, lead show producer for the Tokyo Disneyland Project, was part of a talented Imagineering team that came up with a totally new attraction and restaurant concept for the Disney theme park. Based on Winnie the Pooh and Alice in Wonderland characters, the creative project involved two phases. The first was a theme restaurant called the “Queens of Hearts Banquet Hall.” The second was a major ride attraction based on Winnie the Pooh characters. Both concepts required considerable persuasion to win approval. Traditionally, the Japanese park owners had accepted only attractions that had proved technically successful in other theme parks. Naturally, they were reluctant to try a restaurant concept and a ride technology that were both brand new. Selling the Japanese on the new concepts required oral presentations from Jon Georges and the Imagineering team. Understanding the audience and anticipating its reaction were integral part of Jon’s preparation for a presentation. For the Tokyo Disneyland project, Jon and the Imagineering team wanted to present their concepts in broad terms to see if the financiers liked the total idea. But Jon also knew that this audience would be detail oriented. “Japanese tend to want particulars — like the colour of the concrete, the number of restrooms, and the exact location where visitors would exit an attraction.” Other adaptations Jon made for the Tokyo presentation involved choice of language and presentation style. Carefully avoiding Disney and design jargon, he consciously used common words and simple sentences, which the translator had little trouble converting to Japanese. In making his presentation, Jon kept in mind three important elements: organization, visuals, and focus. Although he had thousands of details in mind, he forced himself to keep his presentation logical and simple. He concentrated on one powerful point: convincing his: Japanese listeners that the new attractions would enhance the value of Tokyo Disneyland and would draw more visitors through the turnstiles. 1. What questions was Jon Georges asking himself in anticipating the audience for the Tokyo Disneyland presentation? 2. Why is simplicity important in an oral presentation and why was it particularly important for the Tokyo Disneyland presentation? 3. Generating and implementing new ideas for the Disney theme parks are tasks of Walt Disney Imagineering, the research, design, and engineering subsidiary of Walt Disney Attractions. Although Tokyo Disneyland is a Disney theme park and Disney retains the creative control of the park, the park is actually owned and operated by the Oriental Land Company. This company makes all financial and investment decisions. While creative concepts come from Disney Imagineering teams, those ideas are not automatically accepted by theme park owners. Imagineering teams not only had to dream up exciting concepts for the Tokyo park, but they also had to sell the ideas and PTC Ly win the approval of Japanese owners. Millions of dollars of contracts and hundreds of jobs in the United States and in Japan rested on successful presentations to the owners of Tokyo Disneyland. Jon Georges, lead show producer for the Tokyo Disneyland Project, was part of a talented Imagineering team that came up with a totally new attraction and restaurant concept for the Disney theme park. Based on Winnie the Pooh and Alice in Wonderland characters, the creative project involved two phases. The first was a theme restaurant called the “Queens of Hearts Banquet Hall.” The second was a major ride attraction based on Winnie the Pooh characters. Both concepts required considerable persuasion to win approval. Traditionally, the Japanese park owners had accepted only attractions that had proved technically successful in other theme parks. Naturally, they were reluctant to try a restaurant concept and a ride technology that were both brand new. Selling the Japanese on the new concepts required oral presentations from Jon Georges and the Imagineering team. Understanding the audience and anticipating its reaction were integral part of Jon’s preparation for a presentation. For the Tokyo Disneyland project, Jon and the Imagineering team wanted to present their concepts in broad terms to see if the financiers liked the total idea. But Jon also knew that this audience would be detail oriented. “Japanese tend to want particulars — like the colour of the concrete, the number of restrooms, and the exact location where visitors would exit an attraction.” Other adaptations Jon made for the Tokyo presentation involved choice of language and presentation style. Carefully avoiding Disney and design jargon, he consciously used common words and simple sentences, which the translator had little trouble converting to Japanese. In making his presentation, Jon kept in mind three important elements: organization, visuals, and focus. Although he had thousands of details in mind, he forced himself to keep his presentation logical and simple.
